item.title: Managing Crisis Projects
item.description: An organization must be accountable, responsive, and integrate understanding in a crisis situation for appropriate management. It is important to understand the difference between risks and unknowns and how to approach their management differently (Paladin Risk, 2014). Project risk denotes factors that may benefit or negate the viability of maintaining the project’s baseline and successfully completing deliverables within constraints, most often scope, cost, and schedule (Meyer et al, 2002). Unknowns are defined as unforeseeable occurrences (Darnall et al, 2018). Unforeseen circumstances may still be addressed through proper understanding of crisis management (Paladin Risk, 2014). Crisis management is defined as “a significant threat to operations that can have negative consequences if not handled properly” (Coombs, 2007). Failing to consider these factors and how they correlate to the life-cycle phases of a crisis may determine that the organization are villains in the eyes of the public instead of the victims of a crisis (Kerzner, 2017). This discernment may determine the fate of an organization.

item.title: Understanding Contracts: CPIF vs FPIF and Procurement Strategy
item.description:
Editor’s note: This is student-era work from May 2022. The contract math in Part 1 has some confused arithmetic (sharing ratios applied as straight divisions, totals that don’t reconcile against the stated targets). It’s preserved as written so the paper reads as the original calculation walkthrough; treat Part 1 as the artifact, not the answer key.

Part 1. Working the Contract Scenarios

1. Cost Plus Incentive Fee Contract

Parameter Value
Target Cost $150,000
Target Fee $25,000
Target Price $175,000
Sharing Ratio 80/20 (80% buyer, 20% seller)
Actual Cost $140,000

Additional Fee = $0. Total Fee Paid = $25,000. Actual cost is under target cost so the incentive fee is awarded.

item.title: Project Charter v2: Nurse Workstation Refresh — Phase 1
item.description:
Notional client project. “Central Medical Center” and “Dr. Phylicia Patterson” are fictional names from the assignment brief. The project mechanics, schedule, budget, risk register, and management language below are my own applied work, presented here lightly edited from the ADMG 474 second-revision charter. The signature block at the bottom is preserved to show the chartering pattern.

Executive Summary

Central Medical Center is a facility with the highest expectation of quality and concern for our community and patients. Recently it has become apparent that our technology for staff and clients is running the risk of failing to meet our organizational vision, values, and mission. For this reason, the initiative to refresh all technology in the facility has been enacted. This first phase of the technology refresh will set the tone for the following stages and bring the organization in line ethically while curtailing future time and cost expenditures.
